name: Bianca Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have answered customer calls and chats at this centre for years. I finished secondary school and handle an ordinary mix of order and payment questions about as well as the next experienced agent. I earn a typical agent wage. I have never used an AI tool; I like to trace the order myself before telling someone what happened.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Leo, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. Leo works at a pharmacy counter, and we have about three months of expenses saved. There are some other centres within reach. I enjoy the regular callers who say I remembered their problem; the part I dislike is being measured as if a reopened case never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau means a few shortcuts, not a new kind of customer. I would still read the order history before telling someone a parcel is lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and wage continue, but three months saved is not enough for every house repair. Leo’s pharmacy job is steady, yet both wages help pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls and checking order records myself. In the first year of minor change, I’d set aside a small amount after each pay for house repairs before buying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about ordinary bills, calm about the work. A lost parcel still needs a person to find the last real address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check for a lost parcel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the address used for the last delivery, not the one printed on an old order. A neighbour once held a parcel because our record copied the wrong house number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save more with three months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo (my partner) and I would keep the repair money separate from school costs. A washing machine can fail in the same week that the children need shoes.

say: I’d say **small shortcuts** do not change the customer’s problem.
I’d insist on the **last delivery address** before calling a parcel lost.
think: I think my **job continues** in this mild case.
I still watch **house repairs** and mortgage bills with three months saved.
do: Keep **taking calls** and checking order histories in 2026.
Set aside **repair money** after each pay in the first year.
S0.quote: A lost parcel still needs a person to find the last real address.
fieldNote: Her **three-month reserve** leaves room for ordinary repairs.
She trusts the **last actual address**, not an old copied one.
She does not use **AI tools** under a mild change.

steps.text: Keep answering calls and tracing parcel addresses through order records
Put a small amount from each pay into a house-repair reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may move standard order answers to software, so management should tell us how many paid shifts remain. I would ask who fixes a wrong delivery answer after the customer calls again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my experience with ordinary cases may not be enough if those cases disappear. Three months saved gives us a short search, and nearby centres could be cutting the same calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written paid-hour figures and keep a list of reopened parcel cases. In the first year standard answers move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaint role at a nearby centre only if its written wage and hours cover our mortgage, while keeping my current shift until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know how to handle a customer, but I cannot make the centre keep the same number of desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which reopened cases would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the calls that return because the parcel was sent to an old address. If the manager says the machine is faster, I would ask how many second calls it created.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend a required demonstration during work hours. I would not buy an AI course without a posted paid job that asks for it.

say: I’d ask management for **written paid-hour figures** before the routine order queue moves.
I’d ask who fixes **wrong delivery answers** when customers call back.
think: I think my **ordinary-case experience** may lose value.
I fear **nearby centres** may be cutting similar calls.
I need a **signed offer** before risking our mortgage on another centre.
do: Request **paid-hour figures** and log reopened parcels in 2026.
Seek **posted complaint work** with written mortgage-covering wage and hours in the first year.
S1.quote: I know how to handle a customer, but I cannot make the centre keep the same number of desks.
fieldNote: She counts **second calls** as a cost of wrong answers.
She limits tool exposure to **required work-time demos**.
A move requires **written mortgage-covering terms** and a signed offer.

steps.text: Keep logging reopened parcel cases and ask for paid-hour figures
Apply for posted nearby complaint work only with written mortgage-covering wage and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do our calls and account checks cheaply, before robots reach hands-on jobs. I would ask for named paid openings and written notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my contact-centre job could end in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not buy me another three years, and three months saved would disappear quickly under the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for the staffing dates in writing and pause buying a new sofa. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid reception role only if its written wage and hours cover the mortgage, and take a funded course only if required for that vacancy on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three months of mortgage money is a short calendar when a headset job can end in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the sofa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leo (my partner) the old sofa is sound even if its fabric is worn. I would rather keep the money for the house than sit on a new one worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make training worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the job posting and wage before a course. If there is no paid opening, I would keep searching rather than pay for a certificate with no clear use.

say: I’d ask for **written staffing dates** and named paid openings.
I’d say **2028 thinking AI** threatens calls before robots.
think: I think my **centre job could end** in 2028.
I know **three months saved** would shrink quickly under our mortgage.
do: Defer the **sofa purchase** and request staffing dates in 2026.
Apply for **posted reception work** after 2028 with written mortgage-covering wage and hours.
Take a **funded course** on paid time only if required for that posted reception vacancy.
S2.quote: Three months of mortgage money is a short calendar when a headset job can end in 2028.
fieldNote: She anchors the risk at **2028 thinking AI**.
The **sofa delay** keeps mortgage cash available.
She rejects **course fees** without a real paid opening.

steps.text: Keep the worn but sound sofa to protect mortgage money
Apply for posted reception work with written mortgage-covering wage and hours after 2028
Take a funded course on paid time only if required for the posted reception vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives enough time to see which posted jobs have actual wages and which are just talk. I would ask for a paid training path before I leave my current shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might learn complaint review over five years if an employer pays for the course. But the same thinking AI could later do that review, so I would not call it permanent safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded complaint-review course on paid time only if a posted paid role requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if its written wage and hours cover our mortgage, keeping my current shifts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to check a real posting. A course without a paid complaint-review job is another bill, not a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the employer for the vacancy, starting hours and who pays for study time. If those are not written down, I would keep taking calls instead of enrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leo check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leo (my partner) the offer must keep our mortgage paid and let us collect the children after school. A higher hourly rate with a shorter week could fail that test.

say: I’d ask employers for **posted wages** before leaving my current call shifts.
I’d seek **paid training** tied to a real role.
think: I think I could learn **complaint review** over five years.
I know **thinking AI** could later reach that role too.
do: Take a **funded review course** on paid time only for a posted role.
Apply after 2031 for **posted review work** with written mortgage-covering wages, hours and pickup schedule; keep current shifts until signing.
S3.quote: A course without a paid complaint-review job is another bill, not a bridge.
fieldNote: She seeks **funding and paid time** for a named course.
The offer must preserve **mortgage and school pickup**.
She rejects **higher hourly rates** if weekly pay falls.

steps.text: Take funded complaint-review course on paid time only for a posted paid role
Apply for posted review work only with written mortgage-covering wage, hours and school-pickup schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives ten years to compare paid jobs while keeping the children settled. I would ask the centre for annual figures on real agent hours, not just answered calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep working and saving for years, though thinking AI may still take the calls in 2036. Robots come around 2039 and do not change the earlier desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls and add a fixed amount to savings after each pay. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid complaint role only if my call hours fall and its written wage and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but the mortgage feels manageable this month. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to compare jobs without betting our home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which annual number matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many hours agents were paid, not how many customers the software answered. A busy screen can hide a thinner rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children at their school unless Leo (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a route we could manage. A different centre nearby is easier than a move.

say: I’d ask for **annual paid agent hours**, not only the number of answered calls.
I’d say ten years lets families **compare real jobs**.
think: I think I could **earn and save** before 2036.
I still see **2036 thinking AI** as a threat to calls.
do: Keep **taking calls** and save a fixed amount from each pay.
Apply for **posted complaint work** after 2036 if hours fall and wages cover mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, manageable bills now.
S4.quote: A busy screen can hide a thinner rota.
fieldNote: She wants **paid hours**, not software call volume.
A family move requires a **signed offer** and school route.
She expects to search **nearby centres** before changing her children’s school.

steps.text: Keep taking call shifts while they remain paid
Add a fixed amount from each pay to household savings
Apply for posted complaint work if hours fall and written wage and hours cover mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the same system could take our simple and difficult calls before I have changed work. Three months saved will not cover a long mortgage gap. I would need written notice, a posted paid role with enough hours for the mortgage, and paid training only if that role really requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks an answer after a customer calls back. A fast chat close can leave a customer with the same wrong bill and another hour on the phone.

headlineQuote: A fast chat close can leave a customer with the same wrong bill and another hour on the phone.
portrait: At **43**, Bianca is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school on typical pay.
She and Leo support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three months saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and prefers to trace orders herself.
She wants **written notice** and a paid, posted role before moving away from calls.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her call wage and exhaust three months of savings during a long search.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, posted mortgage-covering work and required paid training would help.
